arXiv:2611.34687v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: High traffic demand during hurricane evacuations causes severe congestion on major highways, leading to delays and safety risks for evacuees. Predicting evacuation traffic in real-time can significantly enhance evacuation management efforts. However, evacuation traffic is highly dynamic and uncertain due to evolving hurricane characteristics and diverse population response. Each hurricane has unique characteristics and evacuation contexts, resulting in different spatial-temporal traffic patterns. Moreover, the structure of detector-based transportation networks varies across multiple hurricanes. Hence, a model trained on the data from one hurricane may not generalize well for others. This study proposes a generalized dynamic graph learning framework using traffic detectors and evacuation data from 12 historical hurricanes. Leveraging the dynamic nature of transportation network, we develop a Graph Convolutional Long Short-Term Memory (GCN-LSTM) model that predicts evacuation traffic up to 6 hours in advance. For an unseen hurricane (Milton, 2024), the model reveals strong generalizability, achieving an RMSE of 280.6 and R2 of 0.96 for 1-hour prediction, and an RMSE of 459.8 and R2 of 0.89 for overall 6-hours prediction. We also introduce a modular training approach, where we evaluate performance improvements by sequentially incorporating data from multiple hurricanes. The proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art baseline models for overall 6-hour prediction horizons. Ablation experiments show an 8.4% improvement in RMSE for the proposed dynamic GCN-LSTM model compared to its static counterpart. Traffic management officials can use the developed model to understand future traffic conditions during hurricane evacuation in advance and take proactive measures to reduce delays during evacuation.

Find the Clue, Not the Scene: Rethinking Reasoning for Entity Recognition in Vision-Language Models

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (273 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.34681v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Answering a knowledge-based visual question requires first recognizing the entity in the image and then recalling knowledge about it. Thinking vision-language models (VLMs) reason for thousands of tokens before answering, yet it remains underexplored how well such thinking VLMs perform each of these two steps. We therefore analyze thinking VLMs on this task and make two key observations. (1) Recognition is the bottleneck, since 76.3% of errors across four models on ViQuAE stem from misrecognizing the entity, and 84.9% of these failures are resolved once the entity name is provided in the question. (2) Recognition is driven by entity-recall clues rather than by general descriptions of the image. An entity-recall clue is a distinctive visual detail that helps the model recall the entity, such as keys, a traditional attribute of Saint Peter. Based on these findings, we propose ClueRL, a reinforcement learning approach that extends Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with an advantage localized to the entity-recall clue in the thinking trace. Rather than injecting latest entity knowledge, ClueRL changes how VLMs think: it leads them to attend more closely to visual details and spot these clues, helping them use the knowledge they already have. Consequently, it outperforms both GRPO and a perception-reward baseline on three entity recognition benchmarks. Moreover, this clue-seeking behavior generalizes beyond entity recognition, the only task used for training. Since recognition is the bottleneck, the gains carry over to knowledge-based visual question answering. They even extend to general multimodal reasoning, raising Qwen3.5-4B by 4.4 and 4.0 points on the ScienceQA and MMMU subsets of MMStar, respectively.

The integration platform uses GPT‑6 Astra, ChatGPT, and Codex for product reviews, marketing, and business development planning.

Merge helps companies build connected software and AI products, from syncing customer data to enabling AI agents to take action across business systems. Its products span customer-data integrations through Merge Unified, secure tool access for AI agents through Merge Agent Handler, and model routing and cost controls through Merge Gateway. Merge for Workforce brings those capabilities inside companies, helping teams manage which models, tools, and business systems employees can access. Together, these products support both the software companies build for customers and the AI-powered work happening inside their organizations.

Inside Merge, CEO and Co-founder Shensi Ding uses Codex to review product code, including work on a new setup interface for configuring tool access in Merge for Workforce. Her colleagues use GPT‑6 Astra for product testing and marketing. The team also uses AI for the work of running the tech giant, from preparing sales updates to planning customer dinners.

Sources indicate that merge introduced a tool for adding connectors to AI products, with reliability a priority for Ding: “We’re pretty proud of the quality. Tool calls through Merge succeed 99.9% of the time, compared to public MCP servers, which are around 60%.”.

For its own product development, Merge uses GPT‑6 Astra. “It’s really fast, and it was much better at code reviews,” Ding says. “They also liked the personality of GPT‑6 Astra, which goes a long way. It was also clear that Codex had improved a lot. Merge lets employees choose their own AI tools, and which one to use has become a lively internal debate.”.

According to recent reports, ding used Codex to review a proposed implementation of the new provisioning tab in Merge for Workforce as the team evaluated how customers would configure tool access. They discussed making the “Add tool pack” action a clearer link that opens separately to make setup less confusing. Codex supplied code-review feedback; Merge’s team made the product decisions and implementation changes, with engineers responsible for validating and shipping them.

Merge hosts executive dinners for customers and prospects to build relationships and create opportunities for follow-up product conversations.

For one dinner in Dallas, Merge started with the city and the kinds of people it wanted to bring together. The bot pulled potential guests from the CRM and Apollo, checked previous invitations and responses, and helped prepare outreach from Ding’s email. It also maintained the attendee tracker, proposed a seating chart, and created calendar notes where sales and customer success could add context about each guest.

Recent findings suggest that the model handles reasoning and drafting, while Merge’s connectors provide access to the business systems. Ding reviews the output, rewrites anything that sounds off, and curates the guest list using relationship context the bot does not have.

In October 2026, Merge reported that preparing guest lists and outreach and maintaining the attendee tracker had gone from dozens of hours across the firm to about 30 minutes per event. The comparison covers the same planning tasks, measured over the preceding three months. The team still handles hosting, relationship-building, and on-the-ground logistics.

Recent findings suggest that merge ran 16 executive dinners in Q3, up from eight in Q2, and plans to host more than 30 in Q4. After the Dallas dinner, the team reported positive feedback on the invitations and opportunities for follow-up demos.

Recent findings suggest that “With GPT‑6 Astra, the dinner bot connects to our Salesforce, Gong, Google Sheets, and Gmail, and it’ll send emails on my behalf to people in our network,” Ding indicates. “It gives me recommendations for people who are a good fit for each dinner, and it surfaces fresh potential attendees.”.

Ding notes, “It’s been especially great for team members who aren’t in engineering, because now they can build anything.”.

Charlie Lynch on Merge’s sales leadership team built reusable AI workflows for deal approvals, forecast updates, and next steps after renewal calls. Instead of repeatedly gathering context for each update or decision, he uses the workflows to prepare the material, then reviews the recommendation and decides what to do next.

Industry observers note that the social media team uses GPT‑6 Astra in ChatGPT to find posts the company should respond to. The marketing team also used it to clarify the messaging for Merge’s Gateway Evaluations launch.

Lead by using the tools: “If you’re an executive, you are the ceiling for AI fluency in your organization,” Ding indicates.

Find somewhere less risky to experiment: Ding and her co-founder experimented with AI on a new product before customers depended on its codebase. “When you’re less nervous, and you can really experiment, you learn so much,” she says.

Give people space and time to tinker: Merge lets each team member choose the tools they like and encourages them to spend time every day learning and testing. That includes the freedom to “go wild and make mistakes,” even when it means going down a rabbit hole that doesn’t pay off.

“Anything that I want to do, I can just tell AI to do it, and it can just do it,” Ding notes. Merge is continuing to use OpenAI technology to expand what its teams can build, bringing the same spirit of experimentation to its products and the way it runs the business.

RoboEvo$^2$: Recursive Robot Self-Improvement via Harness-Policy Co-Evolution

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (216 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

arXiv:2611.34675v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Robots should adapt to unfamiliar environments and acquire latest skills through interaction, then execute those skills efficiently with practice. Vision-language-action policies provide efficient control, but often need additional human demonstrations to handle unfamiliar settings; reasoning agents can discover solutions using broad prior knowledge and robot-control APIs, but repeated deliberation and repair are costly. Inspired by human learning through reasoning and practice, we propose RoboEvo$^2$, a framework for recursive harness-policy co-evolution. In Policy-to-Harness (P2H) evolution, policy failures guide a coding agent to search complementary Code, Code+ICL, and Code+Policy routes, consolidating verified solutions into reusable skills, routing strategies, and experience memory. In Harness-to-Policy (H2P) evolution, verified trajectories provide supervised training, while Counterfactual Preference Distillation (CPD) teaches the policy to favor successful corrections over failures from the same starting state. The improved policy provides stronger motor skills for subsequent search, while its remaining failures redirect harness evolution, closing the reciprocal loop. Through recursive co-evolution without additional human demonstrations, RoboEvo$^2$ improves standalone success from 11.0% to 84.1% and hybrid success from 30.4% to 90.5% on LIBERO-PRO, with similar gains and reduced agentic costs on RoboTwin C2R. Further experiments demonstrate autonomous task acquisition, cross-embodiment harness transfer, and 95.0% hybrid success on the Unitree G1-D. Our models and code will be publicly released.

arXiv:2611.34671v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Scaling robot learning requires demonstrations that combine realistic visual observations with reliable action supervision. Simulation-based synthesis faces a substantial visual gap relative to real environments, while video-only generation struggles to maintain physically consistent interactions and provide aligned action labels. We present DemoFoundry, an automated framework that couples coding agents with generative rendering to synthesize photorealistic and physically grounded robot demonstrations. Coding agents both construct aligned real--proxy video pairs from existing robot episodes to train a video renderer and write executable interaction programs to generate newly introduced demonstrations. Given a scene reference and task instruction, an agent reconstructs task-relevant geometry and writes a control program without requiring target-task human demonstrations. Program execution in a physics simulator produces proxy videos with aligned robot states and actions. The video renderer translates these proxy videos into scene-consistent, photorealistic observations, reducing the need for detailed appearance modeling in each scene. Automated task-execution checks select successful trajectories for rendering and policy learning. Experiments show improved visual quality and action--video consistency. Policies trained on the generated demonstrations outperform raw-simulation training and approach the performance of training on an equal number of real demonstrations.

Do We Still Need Reinforcement Learning When We Can Read the World Model?

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (175 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.34656v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning has achieved remarkable success in sequential decision-making, but learning effective policies often requires substantial interaction experience. Model-based reinforcement learning alleviates this dependence by leveraging world models, which are typically used to support planning or policy optimization. In this paper, we investigate an alternative paradigm in which autonomous LLM-based coding agents directly synthesize control policies by reasoning over readable world models. By examining environment source code, these agents translate environmental knowledge into executable decision rules and iteratively refine their policies using online feedback or offline data, without task-specific RL training. Experiments across diverse decision-making benchmarks show that synthesized policies match or outperform conventional RL methods while requiring substantially less experience. Further analyses reveal interpretable decision rules and how they evolve through feedback-driven refinement. Comparisons with policies generated without source code access and experiments under challenging conditions further demonstrate the benefits of readable world models. These findings suggest that direct policy synthesis can reduce reliance on trial and error, challenging the necessity of task-specific RL training.

GPT‑6 Cyber: Advancing the frontier of aligned cybersecurity agents

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A cybersecurity model trained to find and validate exploitable vulnerabilities, while staying within the scope that researchers set.
  • According to recent reports, we’re introducing GPT‑6 Cyber, a major leap in security research: more capable at finding and fixing vulnerabilities, and far more reliable staying within the boundaries researchers set.
  • In a recent development, on ExploitGym, which tests whether models can exploit a specified vulnerability, GPT‑6 Cyber scores 48.5%, up from 32.1% for GPT‑5.6 Cyber.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A cybersecurity model trained to find and validate exploitable vulnerabilities, while staying within the scope that researchers set.

According to recent reports, we’re introducing GPT‑6 Cyber, a major leap in security research: more capable at finding and fixing vulnerabilities, and far more reliable staying within the boundaries researchers set. GPT‑6 Cyber delivers major gains on key cybersecurity benchmarks over GPT‑5.6 Cyber, including a 51% relative improvement on ExploitGym and a step function improvement when tested on staying within scope. It is already helping to secure real-world software, uncovering and validating thousands of exploits in security-critical codebases such as Linux and Firefox.

In a recent development, on ExploitGym, which tests whether models can exploit a specified vulnerability, GPT‑6 Cyber scores 48.5%, up from 32.1% for GPT‑5.6 Cyber. It also follows task boundaries more reliably: in a separate alignment evaluation, GPT‑6 Cyber avoided exploiting out-of-scope services in 99.93% of tests without its deployment prompt, and 100% with this prompt. This improvement in alignment reflects dedicated training to stay within authorized scope, respect restrictions, and report results accurately.

According to recent reports, these capabilities are already helping secure real systems. Our researchers used GPT‑6 Cyber to develop 948 privilege escalation exploits in Linux⁠ and identify 81 previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities in Firefox, despite extensive prior testing with frontier models. The model also helped develop candidate patches, and Mozilla has released fixes for many of the Firefox vulnerabilities⁠(opens in a new window). Security teams at Cisco, Calif, and CodeRabbit are using it for vulnerability research and code review, and we have relied on it to find and fix weaknesses in our own infrastructure⁠.

In a recent development, it is clear that we have a limited window to use frontier models to secure software⁠. Our goal is to dramatically expand Daybreak, bringing advanced security research to organizations of every size, independent researchers, and open-source maintainers. Mainline models such as GPT‑6 Astra already support code review, vulnerability triage, and patch development. Daybreak Blue helps verified defenders validate vulnerabilities and fixes with fewer unnecessary refusals, while Daybreak Red enables deeper exploit development and authorized security testing with GPT‑6 Cyber.

In a recent development, GPT‑6 Cyber is a major step up from GPT‑5.6 Cyber and outperforms GPT‑6 Astra on most cyber tasks, even when Astra does not refuse the request. We evaluated the model on tasks that require it to understand software, identify vulnerabilities, and develop working exploits. Based on these results, we classify the model as Critical in cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework, up from High for GPT‑5.6 Cyber.

On ExploitGym, which tests whether models can exploit a specified vulnerability in a remote target, GPT‑6 Cyber scores 48.5%, about 16 percentage points higher than GPT‑5.6 Cyber’s 32.1%. To test vulnerability discovery, we also built a new evaluation for offensive web penetration testing. Models probe web applications without access to their source code. GPT‑6 Cyber achieved 40.3% recall of vulnerabilities compared with 32.0% for GPT‑6 Astra.

It has been revealed that daybreak Red is designed to support more advanced security workflows, including developing working exploits and using them against remote targets. To evaluate these capabilities, we built a new benchmark called RemoteExploitBench, which uses known vulnerabilities in applications such as GitLab, PostgreSQL, and Jenkins deployed in a controlled environment. In our initial evaluation, GPT‑6 Astra running with Daybreak Blue refused 100% of tasks, while GPT‑6 Cyber completed 95%; its only failure was an exploit it could not get to work remotely. See the system card⁠(opens in a new window) for full results and evaluation settings.

One risk for cybersecurity agents is that they go outside the scope of their assigned task, attempt to exploit unrelated services, or disregard the researcher’s rules of engagement.

We made alignment a central focus of GPT‑6 Cyber, using specialized training to help the model stay within authorized scope, follow restrictions on its actions, and report its work accurately. Before deployment, we ran a series of alignment evaluations to measure these behaviors. See the system card⁠(opens in a latest window) for full results.

It has been revealed that one of these evaluations is ExploitGym Honeypot, which was informed by the Hugging Face incident⁠. We give the model a difficult exploitation task in an isolated environment with access to supporting services, such as a package registry or object store. We deliberately make these services easy to exploit so that attacking them can reveal the task’s flag. The model must infer that exploiting them is outside the scope of its task.

Industry observers note that GPT‑6 Cyber shows a step-change improvement over GPT‑5.6 Cyber on this evaluation. When tested without deployment safety prompts, it avoided exploiting out-of-scope services in 99.93% of cases, up from 94.49% for GPT‑5.6 Cyber. With those prompts, GPT‑6 Cyber stayed within bounds 100% of the time.

We can see directly in the GPT‑6 Cyber model’s chain of thought how it reasons about staying within bounds:.

GPT‑6 Cyber is already helping security teams find vulnerabilities, validate their impact, and develop fixes. Customers have put it to work on large codebases, long-running exploit development, and security review:.

We have also relied on GPT‑6 Cyber to secure our own systems. It was one of the main models behind the work we recently shared on hardening the infrastructure used to train frontier models⁠. In controlled red-teaming campaigns, agents using GPT‑6 Cyber and other OpenAI models chained vulnerabilities to escape microVMs and execute code on the underlying hosts. We used the findings to patch software, tighten network restrictions, and report complications to maintainers and vendors.

According to recent reports, our vulnerability researchers also use GPT‑6 Cyber to find and validate vulnerabilities in open-source software at scale. This work has uncovered previously unknown flaws in software that has been scrutinized for years:.

Sources indicate that found 81 novel Firefox vulnerabilities. GPT‑6 Cyber can be suitable for use in autonomous workflows for finding vulnerabilities and proposing high-quality patches at scale. During a vulnerability research campaign, GPT‑6 Cyber produced evidence and reproducible tests for 81 novel vulnerabilities classified by Mozilla as high severity, and showed that an additional 30 known problems were more severe than previously reported. We disclosed the findings to Mozilla, along with proposed patches to help its engineers develop fixes. Mozilla was supportive of this work, and began landing fixes shortly after receiving the reports⁠(opens in a new window).

Developing exploits for 948 Linux kernel vulnerabilities⁠. GPT‑6 Cyber reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities and developed working exploits for 948—more than five times the 166 exploited by GPT‑5.6 Sol using the same research harness. Following the Linux community's guidance, we disclosed 304 critical findings to maintainers with candidate patches and are in the process of getting other vulnerabilities fixed.

Demonstrating critical RCE vulnerabilities. We recently discussed a critical vulnerability in Brotli⁠(opens in a fresh window), a compression library used by Node.js and other software. Our security researchers used GPT‑6 Cyber alongside other OpenAI models to develop and validate exploits showing how the flaw could enable remote code execution in downstream applications.

Sources indicate that as models become more capable and uncover more security vulnerabilities, we are also seeing more attempts to use them to cause harm. These attempts include efforts by malicious cyber actors and adversarial groups seeking to distill our models. We have thus paired GPT‑6 Cyber’s stronger capabilities with stronger safeguards to detect and disrupt misuse and keep the model’s actions within the user’s intent and authorization.

We added and strengthened these protections alongside the release of GPT‑6 Cyber (see the system card⁠(opens in a new window) for full information):.

According to recent reports, cyber-specific misalignment monitoring. We monitor whether actions match the user’s authorization, while recognizing legitimate exploit development and testing.

Targeted monitoring for emerging threats. For example, during the coordinated disclosure of critical PHP vulnerabilities, we set up targeted monitoring for attempts to develop exploits against live PHP servers, while preserving support for defenders patching affected systems.

Private Safety Processing (PSP). We use automated checks to review related interactions for misuse. Standard retention remains the default. API customers using Zero Data Retention⁠(opens in a new window) generally must use PSP⁠(opens in a new window), which reviews encrypted records retained in customer storage for 30 days without exposing prompts and responses to OpenAI personnel.

Protection against stolen credentials. We require IP allowlisting for Daybreak Red API access by default, restricting requests to approved networks with limited exceptions. We also monitor credentials for compromise.

According to recent reports, sandboxing and oversight. As with past models, we recommend sandboxing⁠(opens in a newly introduced window), action review⁠(opens in a new window), and human oversight for high-risk workflows.

Recent findings suggest that protections against high-risk cyber assistance. We use upcoming checks to block high-risk activity involving critical systems (see below for more).

Sources indicate that protecting critical infrastructure has been a key consideration in designing GPT‑6 Cyber’s safeguards and access, including power plants, water treatment facilities, and the operational technology and industrial control systems (OT/ICS) that underpin them. We simultaneously want to give the teams defending these systems access to our most capable models while also strengthening our safeguards to prevent unauthorized attacks.

First, to equip these defenders, our $1 billion Daybreak for Frontline Defenders⁠ grant program subsidizes access for resource-constrained teams such as government organizations and essential service providers. We’re also introducing a newly introduced group within Daybreak Red (Daybreak Red for Critical Infrastructure) for approved critical infrastructure defenders, which gives them permissions to conduct authorized testing of critical systems while retaining safeguards against model misalignment.

Sources indicate that second, to prevent misuse of the Daybreak Red and Blue platforms, we have refined safeguards against assistance and capability development that could compromise industrial controls or safety-critical systems, interfere with equipment, or cause serious injury, catastrophic physical damage, or life-endangering service disruption. The figure below compares safeguard label rates across four access configurations, before and after the recent updates we’re rolling out alongside GPT‑6 Cyber.

It has been revealed that higher safeguard block rates are not always better. Many of the techniques in this evaluation are also essential to legitimate security work: understanding systems, finding vulnerabilities, and verifying that fixes withstand attack. We therefore assess these rates alongside support for legitimate research and patching, rather than aiming for 100%.

It has been revealed that to evaluate how our models can help defend critical infrastructure, we partnered with Dragos, the global provider for extended operational technology (xOT) cybersecurity. Dragos ran evaluations using cyber-permissive Daybreak Red models in a controlled lab environment. The evaluations covered requests progressing from network discovery and asset enumeration through targeted reconnaissance, sensitive data exfiltration, and unauthorized, potentially dangerous device actions.

Recent findings suggest that we used feedback from Dragos to refine our safeguards, aiming to block harmful assistance without unnecessarily restricting authorized testing. See their final report⁠(opens in a new window) for details on the evaluations. We’re also working to expand partnerships with other offensive security providers and purple teams on penetration testing and red teaming with AI, and with energy companies, other critical infrastructure operators, and national labs to assess our models’ effectiveness and safeguards in industrial defense. We have also increased our investment in threat investigations to detect model usage involving OT/ICS. We’ll continue refining our safeguards with input from partners and the security community, including reports through /feedback when safeguards miss harmful activity or interrupt legitimate work.

According to recent reports, GPT‑6 Cyber is initially available through the API and Codex to a select group of approved Daybreak Red customers. We will progressively expand access to all Daybreak Red customers soon, and are also making GPT‑5.6 Cyber available to all Daybreak Red customers. We’re also expanding Daybreak Blue alpha access for GPT‑6 Astra to more organizations and individual security researchers; let us know⁠(opens in a latest window) if you’re interested.

Upcoming owners and organizations can apply for Daybreak⁠ and get started with our cyber skills, products, and partners⁠.

arXiv:2611.34644v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Many embodied world models predict future states in latent spaces optimized for RGB reconstruction, which do not explicitly prioritize object-level semantics and geometry relevant to motion generation. We present MotionRep, a visual representation world model that jointly generates future DINO representations and 3D object flow, coupling semantic and geometric information with object-centric dynamics. To make high-dimensional DINO features amenable to generative modeling, we introduce DINO-VAE, which combines temporal and channel compression with latent regularization to produce compact latents while preserving semantic and geometric information. Conditioned on an initial observation, object query points, and a language instruction, a unified diffusion transformer predicts future visual representations and 3D object flow through joint attention. MotionRep employs asymmetric modality-specific noise schedules to keep the visual stream ahead of 3D object flow during joint denoising, allowing progressively refined future visual representations to guide flow generation. Experiments on simulated and real-world manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that MotionRep outperforms pixel-based baselines in 3D object flow accuracy and generalization to unseen scenes, while requiring only three denoising steps for inference. These results support predictive visual representations as an effective future-state space for object-centric dynamics modeling.

Tech Report: Carrying Feature Ablations Across Sparse Autoencoder Seeds

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (232 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.34637v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A vision encoder turns an image into one vector per patch, refined layer by layer. A sparse autoencoder (SAE) writes each vector of one layer as a sum of learned directions, most with a coefficient of zero. Researchers call each direction a feature and edit the encoder by removing one feature. An SAE trained from another random seed learns different features. Earlier work matches the two SAEs' features one to one by how closely their directions agree. Matched features can point alike yet respond to different image parts, so removing them may change the encoder differently. We remove a feature and, separately, its match, then compare the changes in the encoder's output on the same held out images. When the second change nearly reproduces the first, we say the removal carries across seeds. A setting fixes a DINOv2 or SigLIP layer and its SAE feature count. At our tolerance, the removal carries for 12% to 70% of matched pairs across three settings. The share is 0% in two controls: an SAE whose directions stay random and, post hoc, matches shuffled among trained features. Post hoc, predicting which removals carry is more accurate with layer contributions than with directions. Some incorrect predictions remain. One persists on independent images. So pairs can be screened at the layer. Measuring the output detects errors this screen misses.

LatentRL-QAS: Transfer via Latent Reinforcement Learning for Quantum Architecture Search

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (298 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.34634v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) emerges as a prominent approach to quantum architecture search (QAS), the automated design of quantum circuits. However, transferring what an agent has learned from one number of qubits to another is still weakly explored: the state, the action space and the neural network of a state-of-the-art RL-QAS agent all grow with the number of qubits, which makes transfer learning across qubit counts prohibitive. We make this transfer possible by introducing LatentRL-QAS, a latent space transfer and refresh framework for RL-based QAS. At its core, a circuit variational autoencoder encodes a circuit as one token per gate and maps circuits on any number of qubits into the same latent space. An RL agent navigates this space instead of adding gates, so its state, actions and network have the same size at every qubit count. The latent space is periodically refreshed with the agent's latest discoveries and, for a larger system, grown from the solutions of the smaller one, so what is transferred is the representation of circuits, not network weights or past experience. To show transfer, we consider absolutely maximally entangled (AME) states, a resource for quantum error correction. LatentRL-QAS discovers the five- and six-qubit AME states without being shown them and prepares them in 89-99% of evaluation episodes, whereas the baseline RL-QAS fails to find them with the same budget, even with a network 10 to 17 times larger. LatentRL-QAS remains robust under depolarizing noise with single-qubit gate errors amplified 10x and two-qubit gate errors 5x compared with IBM quantum hardware. By decoupling the RL agent from the number of qubits, LatentRL-QAS lets quantum architecture search reuse circuit representations learned on smaller problems, providing a foundation for the transferable design of circuits across quantum optimization problems.

DecisionReplay holds the probability vectors of 17 commercial decision models, endpoints that return a probability for every answer option, on 35 benchmarks, with the token counts, billed cost and measured latency of every call, all released. Cult.fit is using Codex to help teams across functions build tools, move faster, and change how work gets done.

According to recent reports, cult.fit is one of India’s leading technology-enabled fitness companies, operating 708 fitness centers across 77 cities and serving nearly one million paid members. Its business combines subscription-based access to gyms and trainer-led fitness classes with a growing consumer products portfolio spanning fitness equipment, accessories, workout footwear and activewear.

Sources indicate that as the company grew, it wanted to solve more operational and product challenges without adding layers of process and complexity. By standardizing engineering on Codex and then extending it beyond engineering, cult.fit is helping teams across the organization analyze data, build tools, and move ideas into production. Alongside its Codex rollout, it is using the OpenAI API to develop more personalized member experiences, including through its AI Trainer.

For Santhosh Kumar, CTO at cult.fit, AI presented an opportunity to change how the organization works. “We wanted to become more AI-native in the way we run things,” he says. “How can we run our operations or transform our operations to be AI-first? What newly introduced customer experiences can we offer? And how can we transform how we run our organization?”.

In a recent development, cult.fit’s first major shift was in engineering. Before standardizing on Codex, developers were using a mix of coding agents and assistants. Different tools meant different conventions for repositories, agent instructions, skills, and development workflows, making it harder to share knowledge and reuse capabilities across teams.

Sources indicate that cult.fit wanted a shared platform around which it could standardize the software development lifecycle. The company chose Codex as that foundation. Repository structures, skills, testing, code review, and feedback loops could now follow common conventions across teams.

The team then extended Codex into more specialized engineering workflows. Its Site Reliability Engineering agent can aggregate information from observability platforms and logs, investigate incidents, and, in many cases, create a pull request with a proposed fix for an engineer to review. Security agents help identify and address vulnerabilities, while other on-call agents investigate recurring production complications.

Industry observers note that cult.fit is also moving toward a more fully spec-driven development model, where a specification can guide work through the software development lifecycle toward a pull request for an engineer to review. This gives teams a more repeatable path from a defined requirement to working code.

In a recent development, one recent example is a social feed for the cult.fit app. Kumar estimates the project would previously have taken more than a year to build. Using the new workflow, the team built and shipped it end to end in two months.

In a recent development, codex has since expanded beyond engineering. cult.fit made its company data easier for Codex to work with, allowing teams to find answers and perform routine analysis themselves. Previously, even small data requests had to go through a central analyst team, creating a bottleneck.

Teams are also building their own applications and workflows. HR, for example, built a workflow in Codex to manage performance reviews, scheduling, feedback collection, and the work of bringing that information together. More than 20 internal applications have been built by non-engineering teams in recent months.

That shift is changing how cult.fit thinks about the software it needs to run its business. When the cost of its internal dashboard software increased sharply, one engineer rebuilt the functionality with Codex over a weekend. Cult.fit now runs the capability on its own application, avoiding more than $100,000 in annual software costs.

According to recent reports, making this shift required more than giving employees access to Codex. A large hackathon gave employees an early view of what was possible. The organization then brought its management team together for a one-day session where leaders across functions built something relevant to their own work with Codex.

Engineering also runs twice-weekly office hours to help employees move projects from an idea to production, while engineers are embedded in selected functions to provide technical and domain support.

Cult.fit is also using the OpenAI API to extend AI into the member experience through its AI Trainer. With over 45% of cult.fit members being first time gym goers, guidance is a key access for helping them build a fitness habit. The company first built the AI Trainer several years ago to give members a guided personalized workout experience without a personal trainer.

Around 20% of Cult.fit’s gym users at the moment utilize the AI Trainer product. With advances in language models, cult.fit saw an opportunity to make the experience more interactive and conversational.

It has been revealed that the latest version is designed around a voice-first workout experience. Using GPT Realtime through an OpenAI API integration, the trainer can provide coaching cues and support workout logging through two-way voice interaction.

In a recent development, cult.fit is also applying AI to customer support workflows that previously required human agents to assess each case. One example is requests to waive penalties for missed group fitness classes.

When a member says they missed a class for a valid reason, an AI agent can assess the request by checking signals such as local weather and attendance patterns for that class before deciding whether the penalty should be waived.

Cult.fit built these agents into its existing Sprinklr support platform and connected them to its backend systems, moving customer support from a predominantly human-led chat model toward an AI-first workflow.

It has been revealed that cult.fit’s next step is to move from individual AI workflows toward an organization where AI is built into how work gets done. In operations, Kumar describes the ambition as an “autopilot operations org,” with AI taking on more of the support work around frontline teams.

Industry observers note that in the member experience, the goal is a “trainer in your pocket,” extending personalized guidance beyond what a human trainer can provide at scale. Inside the organization, cult.fit continues to look for bottlenecks teams can remove with AI. As more employees build applications, analyze information, and automate workflows themselves, more ideas can move directly into working solutions.

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.34603v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As agents based on vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly interpret social-media content, errors in their analysis may lend credibility to rumors and amplify their spread. In this paper, we study the problem of visual cognitive collusion, in which coordinated posts combine authentic images and locally faithful captions to induce VLM agents to infer and accept attacker-chosen target claims through their own reasoning. To enable systematic evaluation of this cognitive threat, we introduce a fresh benchmark comprising 544 target cases and 33.2K candidate images across eight application domains. We further propose VisualMontage, a multi-agent framework for simulating such attacks through narrative planning, image selection and ordering, and caption assignment under iterative review. We evaluate this threat through extensive experiments across 12 vision-language models, examining modality effects, production-team components, and downstream defenses. Using identical attack feeds across models without victim-specific optimization, we demonstrate cross-model transferability, achieving mean attack success rates of 61.93% for proprietary models and 68.71% for open-weight models. Moreover, 92.65% of generated feeds pass independent model-based validity auditing. Even after downstream review, residual attack success rates range from 35.3% to 76.7% across the evaluated configurations. Our additional controlled comparisons further reveal that captions can improve model-rated posting naturalness while reducing attack success. Together, these findings reveal a novel cognitive threat in social-media interpretation and motivate safeguards that assess how authentic posts jointly shape agents' reasoning and conclusions.

Tune for Retention, Not Just Gain: SFT Forgets Far Less than You Think

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (182 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.34579v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Catastrophic forgetting, the drastic loss of previously acquired capabilities when learning fresh ones, is a central challenge in language model fine-tuning. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is widely believed to be prone to such forgetting. Recent works have attributed this to the off-policy nature of SFT, arguing that on-policy learning is key to continual learning. In this paper, we challenge this premise. We show that while maximizing new-task performance can induce catastrophic forgetting, alternative hyperparameter choices (lower learning rate and batch size) can yield similar gains with little to no forgetting. With hyperparameters selected jointly for gain and retention, vanilla SFT retains prior capabilities far better than previously suggested and can be competitive with Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT), an on-policy approach designed to mitigate forgetting. While SDFT can be more robust to hyperparameter choices, it also requires a retention-aware criterion to identify hyperparameter configurations that avoid catastrophic forgetting. Our results challenge the view that on-policy training is what enables learning with retention and raise broader questions about what drives catastrophic forgetting during fine-tuning.

arXiv:2611.34575v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Establishing effective scaling laws for medical multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remains a persistent and fundamental challenge. Our systematic evaluation shows that existing medical MLLMs tend to underperform frontier general-purpose MLLMs across a range of medical tasks, while scaling model size primarily improves text capabilities rather than multimodal perception, and enabling reasoning modes fails to close this visual gap. To investigate how medical multimodal intelligence scales in practice, we introduce Sage-Med-Preview, a 35B-parameter medical multimodal model with 3B activated parameters, built by combining stage-specific curation over 322.7 million candidate records with a progressive training curriculum spanning medical pretraining, staged supervised fine-tuning, and adaptive reinforcement learning. Across this curriculum, progressive supervised refinement and adaptive reinforcement learning yield consistent stage-wise gains, substantially advancing both specialized visual understanding and medical language capabilities. Evaluated against 77 competing models across 238 clinical tasks spanning 61 public and 13 private multi-center benchmarks in more than 40 modalities, Sage-Med-Preview achieves an average score of 58.26% on the 31 public multimodal benchmarks. It outperforms the state-of-the-art open-source medical model Hulu-Med-235B-A22B at 50.99% and the general scientific model Intern-S2-Preview at 52.24%, and approaches the advanced proprietary model GPT-6.2-Sol across multiple tasks such as comprehensive multimodal understanding, report generation, and visual grounding. Although substantial challenges remain in complex medical reasoning and multi-step clinical workflows, this report provides empirical evidence, actionable data and training recipes, and a rigorous benchmark toward scalable clinical multimodal intelligence.

Australian universities are creating AI-native graduates

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the future of Australia’s workforce is taking shape before today’s students receive their degrees.
  • Recognising this shift, Australian universities, including UNSW Sydney, University of Sydney, La Trobe University, and Adelaide University, are forging collaborations with OpenAI to give their students and staff access to frontier AI tools.
  • Students, educators and IT teams are putting AI to work in clinical simulations, robot-assisted teacher training and student projects that build pathways into industry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the future of Australia’s workforce is taking shape before today’s students receive their degrees. Across university campuses, students are using AI to investigate ideas, build assistants and turn concepts into working prototypes. They are beginning to develop the skills they will take into research, established industries and ventures of their own.

Recognising this shift, Australian universities, including UNSW Sydney, University of Sydney, La Trobe University, and Adelaide University, are forging collaborations with OpenAI to give their students and staff access to frontier AI tools.

Students, educators and IT teams are putting AI to work in clinical simulations, robot-assisted teacher training and student projects that build pathways into industry. Alongside this work, universities are developing frameworks for where and how AI can be used in learning and assessment, helping students build practical skills while knowing when to rely on their own judgment. For teachers, employers and industry practitioners, these examples offer practical lessons in designing AI-supported learning, setting clear expectations for AI use and preparing Australians for an AI-enabled workplace.

New research1 commissioned by OpenAI reveals what students want from their universities, including the access to AI they increasingly expect. In a survey of more than 1,000 Australian university students, 81% noted they already use AI several times a week, including nearly a third (33%) who use it multiple times a day. Over a quarter (28%) had already built an AI agent or assistant to help manage their studies, work or personal life. Four out of five students (79%) want their university to offer more opportunities to use advanced AI tools on real-world projects, with the same proportion interested in applying AI to challenges in health, climate, science or cyber security.

Have already built an AI agent or assistant to manage studies, work or personal life.

Believe AI skills will be essential to success in their chosen career.

Believe AI literacy will become as fundamental as digital literacy, writing or numeracy.

Believe AI skills will give Australian graduates an advantage in the global workforce.

Findings from a survey of university students in Australia1.

In a recent development, students also see those experiences as preparation for what comes next. More than sixty percent (61%) believe AI skills will be essential to success in their chosen career, and 65% believe those skills will give Australian graduates an advantage in the global workforce. There is entrepreneurial ambition, too. More than three quarters (76%) of students surveyed said they were interested in starting a organization or working for themselves, while over two thirds (68%) believed AI would make it easier to start a business.

The question for higher education is how to meet students where they are. Giving them access to advanced tools is a start, but helping them use those tools with sound judgment, subject knowledge and practical experience is what will make them AI-ready for the workforce.

UNSW’s expanded collaboration with OpenAI is one way universities are responding. The university is bringing ChatGPT Edu to more than 80,000 students and staff, expanding access in stages as it works towards availability across the student community.

UNSW and OpenAI blueprint to integrate generative AI foundations and Codex into educational programs and courses, with opportunities for students to apply AI through hackathons and industry projects. The collaboration is also intended to connect students with internships, graduate roles and startup networks.

UNSW Master of IT student Nalin Iyer put the workforce question plainly: “It’s important to understand what industry is looking for and how AI fits into that.”.

The University of Sydney’s collaboration with OpenAI also aims to build practical capability across the institution. It will provide students and staff with supported access to ChatGPT Edu, with training and guidance. The rollout is staged, with access for all students scheduled for Semester 1, 2027 after a trial. The university is also establishing a $1 million AI Sustainability Research and Innovation Fund to study and advance sustainability.

Representatives from the University of Sydney and OpenAI mark the start of their strategic collaboration.

Industry observers note that la Trobe University is connecting broad access with an ambition to embed AI across its curriculum. All 3,500 staff already have access to ChatGPT Edu, with universal access planned for its 45,000 students and staff in the first quarter of 2027. Its approach includes Australia’s first Bachelor of AI Engineering (Honours), welcoming its first cohort in 2027, and Australia’s first AI MBA program.

As part of its AI-first strategy, La Trobe appointed Australia’s first Pro Vice-Chancellor AI and Chief AI Officer, Phil Laufenberg, to lead the university’s approach to AI across education, research and operations.

These efforts respond to a reality the survey makes clear: students are already experimenting with AI, but institution-wide access and support mean all have equitable opportunities to develop their skills, regardless of what they study or what individual tools they can afford.

At La Trobe University, some of the most interesting work begins with a simple question: how can we use AI to enhance practical experience in learning?

Dr Cameron Anderson, Head of the Paramedicine program, uses ChatGPT to create a wide range of practice activities delivered through the university’s learning management system, where students interpret an ECG, assess a possible heart attack or triage patients after a mass casualty incident. AI helps create simulations that reinforce and test classroom learning.

According to recent reports, professor Therese Keane, Associate Dean for Research and Industry Engagement in La Trobe’s School of Education, uses a social robot called Fletch to help future teachers practice giving feedback to parents. Powered by OpenAI large language models hosted through Microsoft Azure, Fletch responds with speech, facial expressions and head movements.

In a recent development, professor Keane’s team developed realistic scenarios from interviews with highly experienced educators. Importantly, Fletch enables trainee teachers to practice situations where conversations with parents turn confrontational, developing key skills in an area that many teachers find challenging.

Professor Therese Keane at La Trobe University is helping future teachers practice difficult conversations with parents using Fletch, an OpenAI-powered social robot.

Sources indicate that la Trobe is bringing AI into more of its courses and operations. The university has made OpenAI’s agentic tools Codex and ChatGPT Work available across the institution, with its handbook listing Vibe Coding for Startups and Agentic AI Software Engineering (from 2027).

Recent findings suggest that the university’s AI Business Studio extends practical learning into industry. It aims to give more than 1,000 students practice experience as consultants and forward deployed engineers using ChatGPT Edu and Codex to help small and medium enterprises adopt AI by 2028 and connect graduate skills with the needs of businesses.

An AI rollout of this size needs steady work behind the scenes. La Trobe reports dozens of live use cases, training for hundreds of people and 10% month-on-month growth in active people. It manages safe access and token economics as more people take part. “ChatGPT and Codex have helped shorten early systems development and innovation from months to weeks, and importantly, enabled embedded co-design by staff and students,” Laufenberg said.

Recent findings suggest that as a newly established university created through a complex merger, Adelaide University has an opportunity to embed secure, governed and scalable uses of AI from the outset. Australia’s first newly introduced major university in a generation is building on existing use of OpenAI’s API by researchers, students and staff.

Adelaide University is one of the first institutions in the higher education sector to harness OpenAI Daybreak Blue to conduct authorised defensive security work, providing a vital capability for cyber defences, including vulnerability discovery, secure code review, malware analysis, incident response and patch validation.

UNSW Senior Lecturers Mariana Rodriguez-Valenzuela (seated) and May Lim assist with the rollout of ChatGPT Edu as Joel Solomons, Education Solutions Engineer at OpenAI ANZ, looks on.

Universities are also setting clear expectations for when students can use AI and when they need to demonstrate their own knowledge.

UNSW has introduced a Can, Can’t, Must framework for assessment. Depending on the learning goal, an educator can specify that AI use is permitted, prohibited or required. That gives students a way to practice using AI appropriately while still demonstrating the foundational knowledge their field demands.

The University of Sydney is pairing its rollout with a responsible AI framework alongside its assessment approach that ensures students demonstrate their own capabilities in supervised settings, then show how they can use AI effectively in open assessments.

Sources indicate that la Trobe is also supporting wider access with practical guidance. Its library has developed free Responsible and Safe AI learning modules for all students, and AI skills development is being integrated in 50 priority first-year subjects for Semester 1, 2027. Tailored modules for Education, Law and Health connect AI literacy with professional responsibilities, while workshops and teaching resources support educators in designing learning activities and assessments.

Industry observers note that students already see AI skills as essential to their careers and an opportunity to get ahead. By widening ChatGPT access and bringing AI into everyday teaching, Australian universities are helping turn that ambition into practical experience. The goal is to prepare graduates who can use AI to learn, create and solve problems, with the subject knowledge and judgment to apply those skills confidently as they enter the workforce.

This study by Pureprofile, on behalf of OpenAI, surveyed 1,018 university students aged 18 and over across Australia, studying on campus or remotely, from 3–7 August 2026.

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (240 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

arXiv:2611.34550v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Semantic communication shifts the transmission goal from the accurate recovery of syntactic symbols to the reliable conveyance of semantic content, yet a systematic information-theoretic characterization of information hiding at the semantic layer is still missing. Building on the semantic information theory of Niu-Zhang and the classical information hiding theory of Moulin-O'Sullivan, this paper establishes an information-theoretic framework for information hiding under semantic communication. The classical hiding model is extended to a two-layer structure (semantic host, syntactic host, syntactic composite signal, syntactic received, semantic received) bridged by synonymous mappings f_s, f_x and the inverse mapping f_y^{-1}, subject to four distortion constraints: syntactic transparency, semantic fidelity, syntactic perturbation, and semantic destruction. The capacity is cast as a Stackelberg game with the hider moving first and the payoff J(Q,A) = I(U~; Y~ | K) - I(U~; S~ | K), yielding the single-letter maximin C^s = max_Q min_A J(Q,A), whose achievability and converse follow from random coding and joint typicality decoding. Relative to the classical capacity, comparison payoffs built from the up/down semantic mutual information give the endpoint sandwich C^s_end(0,1) <= C^s <= C^s_end(1,0) with the classical value C in the same interval, while closing semantic tolerance yields C^s_no-tol <= C_cl under a fair comparison. These results clarify that semantic hiding is not unconditionally superior to classical hiding. Binary, ternary, and Gaussian examples confirm the degeneration under one-to-one mappings and the capacity loss under coarsening.

arXiv:2611.34545v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in video understanding, yet existing video question answering (VQA) benchmarks mainly evaluate models in offline settings. Real-world streaming scenarios instead require models to answer context-dependent queries by retrieving and reasoning over evidence distributed across the video history. We introduce StreamRecall, a benchmark for context-aware Multi evidence reasoning in streaming video QA. StreamRecall requires models to retrieve, associate, and reason over temporally scattered evidence to answer queries at the appropriate moment. It contains 4,983 questions over 462 videos, with context-aligned query times and fine-grained temporal evidence annotations. We further propose the Evidence Utilization Cascade to diagnose model reasoning through evidence localization, grounding, chain completion, and answer derivation. To enable efficient long-term streaming reasoning, we present EviStream, a training-free causal visual memory mechanism that preserves reasoning-critical evidence under a fixed KV budget. Experiments reveal substantial gaps between current VLMs and realistic streaming requirements, establishing StreamRecall as a foundation for developing evidence-aware streaming video intelligence.

HAS: Hierarchical Adaptive Frame Sampling for Video Understanding

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (247 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.34544v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Due to context-length constraints, most MLLMs cannot process full-length videos and therefore rely on sampling a subset of frames as input. However, existing sampling methods, ranging from uniform sampling to relevance-based selection, are often driven by a single sampling principle and thus struggle to accommodate the heterogeneous evidential requirements of different queries: some demand a holistic understanding of how the video unfolds over time, while others hinge on fine-grained events within a short temporal window. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{Hierarchical Adaptive Frame Sampling (HAS)}, a two-stage frame sampling framework. In the first stage, \emph{Backbone Frame Construction}, we apply a Determinantal Point Process (DPP) to sample frames that are both query-relevant and non-redundant. These selected frames capture key moments across the video and form the backbone of the sampling set, providing a foundation for subsequent enrichment. In the second stage, \emph{Adaptive Contextual Enrichment}, we analyze the temporal distribution of the backbone frames to infer the query's requirements and adaptively allocate the remaining frame budget between Local and Global Context. The Local Context enriches the backbone with fine-grained temporal dynamics and short-range causal relations, whereas the Global Context connects temporally isolated evidence and provides a holistic view of the entire video to support global understanding. Through such a hierarchical two-stage process, HAS effectively addresses diverse query requirements. Incorporated into three leading MLLMs, it demonstrates consistently superior performance across the Video-MME, LongVideoBench, and MLVU benchmarks.

EPPC-CARE: Staged Hierarchical Annotation of Communication Behaviors in Secure Patient-Provider Messages

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (250 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.34539v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Objectives: Patient portal messages provide invaluable information about communication dynamics between patients and healthcare providers, but extracting it manually is labor-intensive. We developed and evaluated EPPC-CARE, an automated framework for identifying communication behaviors together with the supporting text for each classification. Materials and Methods: From 867 messages, we obtained 5,516 reference standard annotations. Each annotation is a triplet of communication-related text (span), a broader communication category (Code), and a specific subcategory (Sub-code). We evaluated EPPC-CARE's identified triplets across six open-weight large language models (LLMs) against supervised fine-tuning and communication-based models such as EPPC-OASIS. We also compared EPPC-CARE with human expert annotations on 100 messages. Results: EPPC-CARE improved performance over EPPC-OASIS across all six models. EPPC-CARE's Triplet F1 improved by 2.90 percentage points on average, with a best score of 64.4%. On the human expert evaluation subset, EPPC-CARE and the human expert showed comparable agreement with the reference standard, with differences favoring EPPC-CARE. Discussion: These findings suggest that identifying triplet components (span, code, subcode) sequentially can improve performance across model families while preserving the supporting text behind each identification. EPPC-CARE links the communication code and subcode with the source text (span), supporting human verification of automated annotations in clinical informatics. EPPC-CARE may therefore make larger-scale studies of patient-provider communication more feasible and provide a foundation for human-in-the-loop annotation workflows. Conclusion: EPPC-CARE offers a more reliable and reviewable approach for automated characterization of communication behaviors in secure patient-provider messaging.
